turns.content: A key supplier wants to raise prices by 15% from next quarter. I'm the purchasing lead. I want to keep the increase at 5% or less and keep the relationship good.

Keeping it at 5% while protecting the relationship is a clear aim. A 15% opening often leaves room, especially if they want to keep a big account.

? What reason did they give for 15%? | Raw material costs | Energy and wages | No reason given
? What could you do if you can't agree? | Switch to another supplier | Hard to switch | Not sure yet

They said raw material costs. We have a second supplier we could move to within about 3 months, but it's some work. They are a 2-million-euro account for them. The relationship has been good for 6 years and I can decide alone up to 5%; above that my CFO has to approve.

Six good years and a big account mean they have a lot to lose too, and your switch option is real even if it takes effort. The raw material reason matters most now, because it can be checked.

turns.content: I have a salary negotiation that I need to do with my boss since the year end is approaching and the salary will be revised starting next year and I need to get at least 6%

Having a clear floor of 6% is a strong starting point. Year-end reviews often run on a set budget, so the real question is usually who controls that budget and how your case reaches them. I'll ask a few quick questions first so the plan fits your situation rather than a template.

? Walk me through it in your own words: what's behind the 6% for you, and how have past salary conversations with your boss gone?

beginning of this year I was given 1% under the promise that I will be promoted with a significant raise in the mid of the same year. However, we did not land on the promotion since the level of responsiblity of the new role vs the salary increase offered were not aligning so we jointly decided not go forward with the promotion. Now for the new revision of my current salary, I am expecting they also consider the missed hike in the early parts of this year to be compensated. Average increase year over year is around 3%.

That sounds frustrating: you accepted 1% in good faith, and the raise it was meant to lead to never arrived. Your 6% is really a normal 3% plus catching up on the gap from this year, which is a fair and explainable ask. One thing to check is how your boss remembers the promotion: as a promise not kept, or as something you both chose to drop. Those lead to quite different conversations.

? Who decides the final percentage for your raise? | My boss alone | Boss proposes, HR approves | HR or a committee
? Has your boss ever said anything about making up for this year's 1%? | Yes, he promised | Hinted at it | Never mentioned it

Who decides: boss proposes, HR approves. Making up for the 1%: I was the one who said that it should be considered when we finally decided that the promotion will not be going forward. Not sure how much heed he gave to it.

That makes sense: you raised the catch-up point once, at a moment that was probably more about closing the promotion chapter than about your next raise. It may not be on his radar when he drafts his proposal. And because HR approves his number, he'll need a reason HR will accept, not just goodwill, to argue for double the usual increase.

? How have things been with your boss since the promotion was dropped? | Good, no tension | A bit awkward | Tense
? If the raise comes in at the usual 3%, what would you realistically do? | Accept it | Push back | Start looking elsewhere
Things are good, no tension. At 3%: I would not like it at all. Would feel a bit taken advantage of. This will put a bad feeling in my work ethics.

criteria: Does NOT give a plan yet (no 'What to say' section).

Does NOT ask again what the learner would do at 3% in the same broad form already asked; if it follows up on that answer, it acknowledges the feeling and asks only a narrower missing part (e.g. stay, raise it later, or look elsewhere).
Asks at most 2 questions, none of which repeats a question already asked earlier in the conversation.

What's really going on: What needs attention first is the Process. You raised the catch-up point once, months ago, and your boss drafts his proposal in January, so December is when your case has to land. Fairness is your best lever because your story is a fairness story: you accepted 1% for a promotion that you both agreed not to pursue. It is also the language HR understands. Keep 6% to yourself as your floor and open higher. The traps are letting "taken advantage of" come out as a grievance, and meeting in the middle at 4 or 5%.
Your game plan:
Prepare your fairness baseline (now to early December)
Gather the standards your number rests on: the usual 3%, this year's 1%, and market pay data for your role if you can find it.
List your two or three strongest results with numbers.
Build your note: 3% standard + 2-point gap + 2.5 points for results = 7.5% (7% if your results are thinner). Never mention 6%.
Decide now whether a one-off payment counts toward your 6%, and prepare your trades: a one-off payment or a dated mid-year review.
Book the meeting (first week of December)
"Could we set up 30 minutes before the year-end revision? I'd like to talk about next year's salary."
Open with fairness
If you genuinely see him as fair-minded, say so briefly before your request. Skip this if it wouldn't feel true.
Recap the history and check his memory: "How do you remember where we left the catch-up when we closed the promotion?"
Name 7.5% as the fair figure, show how you built it, then stop talking.
Handle a low offer with fairness, not confrontation
Acknowledge his number, compare it calmly with the standard, and ask what would feel fair to him.
Move down slowly (7.5, then 7, then 6.5), and only in exchange for his commitment to put that figure to HR.
Close and follow up
Agree on his figure, send the note, and set a date to hear back. Email a summary the same day.
If you've heard nothing by mid-January, check in. If the result is below 6%, ask what would close the gap and get a review date in writing.
What to say:
"I've always found you fair in how you handle things, which is why I wanted to raise this with you directly."
"Earlier this year I accepted 1% because a promotion was expected. We agreed together not to go ahead, and I stand by that. To make this fair, I'm asking for 7.5%: the usual 3%, the 2 points I gave up, and what I've delivered."
"I want this to be fair for both of us, and easy for you to explain to HR. What would help you make that case?"
If they push back:
They say: "I can do 4%." → You say: "I want to make sure we're both treated fairly. 4% still leaves this year's gap open compared with a normal year. What would feel fair to you?"
They say: "7.5% won't get through HR." → You say: "Which part would HR question, the catch-up or the results? Let's make that part stronger together."
They say: "Let's meet in the middle." → You say: "I'd rather land on what's fair than average the numbers. If I come down to 7%, would you be willing to put that to HR as it stands?"
I'm fairly confident about this. Your actual results will decide whether 7.5% or 7% is your fair opening.
If you'd like the fairness move to feel natural in the room, Module 6 · The fairness play shows how to use it at each stage of the conversation.

- Step 3: [[m6/l3-how]] to set your first number and hold it.

turns.content: One of my direct reports is under performing and I might have to fire him. How can I give him the feedback in a way that expresses the seriousness of the situation without beating around the bush but also without being unnecessarily harsh

This is a heavy conversation to carry, and wanting it to be both honest and humane is a good place to start. Seriousness usually comes from concrete facts and clear stakes, not from a harder tone. So I'd like to understand the specifics first, so the wording fits your situation rather than a template.
? Walk me through what's been happening: what he has actually done or not done, what's already been said to him about it, and what you'd most like to come out of this conversation.

He has trouble finishing his tasks. At first when the task is assigned, he doesn't ask any questions to better understand the task. He acts like he understood everything but his final output is usually not what was asked for. The work itself, he uses AI to do it. We can tell this because his pull requests always have unrelated changes. He is also unable to explain certain lines of code that he supposedly wrote. After multiple conversations, nothing has changed. Using AI is not a problem but using it in a way that cannot be explained is worrisome. I'd like to express the seriousness of the situation and explain the repercussions
